newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines still wary despite low inflation.
newsitem.headline: Philippines still wary despite low inflation.

text.p: The Philippines' steady 4.8 percent inflation in July brought cheer to the stock market on Tuesday, but analysts remained wary saying the effects of the peso's de facto devaluation may only be felt in succeeding months.
The Manila share index rose 1.39 percent to 2,676.2 points.
"The 4.8 percent is lower than expected. It's possible it would still have a lagged effect. We'll have to see the impact in August," said Lito Dalit, an economist of AsianBank Corp.
A Reuters poll on Monday had predicted annual inflation in July at 5.3 percent.
July inflation was unchanged due to the lower year-on-year rate in the food, beverage and tobacco index at 1.5 percent in July from 1.7 percent in June.
Utilities also slowed down to 7.5 percent from 8.3 percent.
The 4.8 percent inflation in July brought the seven-month average for the year to 4.63 percent.
The Philippine central bank on July 11 allowed the de facto devaluation of the peso after futile attempts at defending the currency from speculators.
Last Friday, the country's three oil firms raised their product prices as almost their entire crude oil requirements are imported.

AsianBank's Dalit said though the government's annual average inflation target of six to seven percent remained achievable, it could rise to nine percent by end of the year due to higher costs of doing business following a weaker peso and higher interest rates.

The central bank had raised interest rates to a 2 1/2 year high of 32 percent in defense of the peso. It has since then brought it down but its overnight borrowing rate still remains at a relatively high 20 percent.

Helen Alvarez, research director of All Asia Capital and Trust Corp, said a higher six-month export figure announced on Tuesday was also encouraging, but investors were likely to be wary because of the volatility in the region's currency markets.
"If the costs of production of exports go up, the depreciation of the peso could still be contractionary in the long term," she said.
"The attitude is to wait and see," Alvarez said, adding that she had so far projected full-year inflation to reach 5.9 percent from an earlier 5.5 percent.
Analysts said they expect the peso, which had fallen 13.6 percent in July, to settle at 28/28.50 to the dollar but the persisting currency volatility in the region could upset it.
The central bank remains optimistic the peso speculation may soon end so it can bring back interest rates to normal levels after putting in place a package of monetary measures.
